code.title: Before and after generics: compile-time checking

followUps: No, generics add no runtime cost compared with hand-written casts. After erasure the bytecode is the same as the Object-based version: List<String> is a plain List and javac inserts the same checkcast you would have typed. The real cost is elsewhere: List<Integer> must box each int into an Integer object, so summing 1 million ints touches 1 million small objects. That boxing is the same in the old Object-based code.

Because type arguments must be reference types, and int is a primitive with no class and no Object parent. Erasure turns T into Object, and an int cannot be stored in an Object variable without boxing. Use List<Integer> and let autoboxing convert int to Integer, or use int[] and IntStream when boxing costs matter. Project Valhalla aims to lift this limit later.

code.title: Type parameter, argument, raw type and diamond

followUps: By convention they are single uppercase letters: T for a type, E for a collection element, K and V for map key and value, R for a result, N for a number. Use T, U, S for second and third types. A short name stands out from class names like String, so the reader sees at once it is a placeholder. Some teams use a descriptive name like TRequest when several parameters exist; it is a convention, not a compiler rule.

No, a static method cannot use the class type parameter, because T belongs to an instance (Box<String> vs Box<Integer>) and a static member is shared by all of them. There is only one static field, not one per type argument. Give the static method its own parameter instead: static <U> Box<U> of(U v) { return new Box<>(v); }. The method's U is inferred at each call, so Box.of(5) returns Box<Integer>.

code.title: Invariant generics versus covariant arrays

followUps: A compile-time check is better, because it catches the bug before the program ever runs. A runtime check only fires on the path that executes: an ArrayStoreException may appear in production after months. A compile-time error is found on every build, on every path, with the line number. The cost is some flexibility: you must use wildcards to say "read-only list of any Number". Runtime checks stay useful as a safety net, for example Collections.checkedList or Class.cast.

It is a supertype of List<Integer>, List<Double>, List<Long> and List<Number> itself, so one parameter can accept any of them. In turn, List<? extends Number> is a subtype of List<?> and Collection<? extends Number>. You may read Number from it, but you may not add anything except null, because the real element type could be Integer and adding 2.5 would corrupt it.

code.title: PECS: copy and sort with wildcards

followUps: Wildcards in a return type force every caller to deal with them. If a method returns List<? extends Number>, the caller can read Number but cannot add to it or assign it to a List<Number>. The flexibility belongs to the parameters, where it helps callers. Return the exact type, List<Integer>, and let the caller widen it if wanted. Bloch says: "do not use bounded wildcard types as return types" (Effective Java, Item 31).

It is the compiler's name for the one unknown type behind a wildcard. For List<?> list, the compiler gives that unknown type a hidden name such as "capture#1 of ?". An error like "incompatible types: Integer cannot be converted to capture#1 of ?" means you tried to add an Integer to a list whose element type is unknown, and nothing but null is guaranteed to fit. Fix it by using a generic helper <T> void f(List<T> l) that captures the type.

code.title: Raw List, List<Object> and List<?>

followUps: Yes. list.clear() and remove(...) compile on a List<?> because they do not need the element type: clear takes no element, and remove takes an Object. What is blocked is anything that passes an element in, such as add(E), where E is the unknown type; only null is accepted. Reading with get(i) gives you Object. So List<?> supports size, iteration, clear, contains and remove.

Yes, List<?> is reifiable: at runtime it is exactly a List and no type information is lost, because nothing was specified. That is why o instanceof List<?> and new List<?>[3] compile, while o instanceof List<String> does not. Unbounded wildcard types are the only parameterized types that are reifiable. The same applies to raw types and to non-generic types.

code.title: Erasure and its workarounds

followUps: C# can reify generics because it was designed with them from version 2.0, and its runtime was changed to carry type arguments. Java added generics in 2004 (Java 5) to a huge existing ecosystem. Erasure meant old and new code could share the same class files and the same ArrayList, and libraries could add type parameters without breaking callers. The price: no new T() or instanceof List<String>. C# paid with a clean break, since its generics libraries were new.

Declarations keep their generic types in the class file's Signature attribute, so reflection can read them. field.getGenericType() returns List<String> for a field declared that way, method.getGenericReturnType() and getGenericParameterTypes() work too, and class.getGenericSuperclass() gives Node<Integer> for class IntNode extends Node<Integer>. What is not kept is the type argument of an object: you cannot ask an ArrayList instance what its E was.

code.title: Bounded type parameter versus wildcard

followUps: Yes, a type parameter can have no lower bound, but a wildcard can. <T super Integer> is a compile error; the language only allows extends on type parameters. You can write ? super T as a wildcard on a parameter, as in Comparator<? super T>, and you can use T itself in a signature that has such a wildcard. Reason: a lower bound on a type variable would give the compiler no method to call on it, since all it would know is Object.

Because after erasure the type variable becomes its first bound, and a class can only be a superclass, not an interface. In <T extends Number & Comparable<T>> the erased type is Number, so the class must come first. Written the other way round, <T extends Comparable<T> & Number> is a compile error. Only one class is allowed, and any number of interfaces can follow after it, joined with &.

code.title: Why Collections.max has a complex signature

followUps: A call such as Collections.max(apples) fails when Apple extends Fruit and only Fruit implements Comparable<Fruit>. With <T extends Comparable<T>>, T would be Apple, which is not Comparable<Apple>, so javac reports an inference error. With Comparable<? super T>, Comparable<Fruit> qualifies since Fruit is a supertype of Apple. The same trap catches java.sql.Timestamp and LocalDate, which compare with a supertype.

Binary compatibility means old compiled .class files still link and run against a newer library. The JDK cares because millions of jars were compiled against Java 1.4. When Collections.max gained generics, its erased signature had to stay Object max(Collection), or every old jar would throw NoSuchMethodError at runtime. The Object & trick keeps that exact descriptor. Rule of thumb: the JDK never removes or changes a public method's erased signature.

code.title: Bridge methods seen through reflection

followUps: Run javap -p -c IntNode (add -v for flags). Without -v you see both void setData(java.lang.Integer) and void setData(java.lang.Object); the second body does checkcast Integer and then invokevirtual setData(Integer). With -v the Object version carries flags: ACC_BRIDGE, ACC_SYNTHETIC. In code, Method.isBridge() returns true for it, which is how frameworks skip duplicates when scanning methods.

Only a little, and usually none after JIT compilation. A bridge adds one extra call and one cast, and the JIT inlines such tiny methods. It does show up as an extra frame in stack traces and can confuse tools that scan methods by reflection, so annotation processors check isBridge(). One famous gotcha: annotations on a method used to be missing on its bridge, which caused Spring and Hibernate bugs before the JDK copied them across in Java 8.

code.title: Heap pollution and checkedList

followUps: It is safe inside ArrayList because the array is private and never leaves the class. The (T[]) new Object[n] cast is erased to Object[], and elements are only read and cast one at a time. If you return that array to a caller as String[], javac inserts a cast to String[] at the call site and it fails with ClassCastException, because the real object is Object[]. Rule: never let the array escape its class.

If your program compiles with no unchecked warnings, the JLS guarantees that heap pollution cannot occur, so the casts javac inserts will never throw ClassCastException. Put differently, a ClassCastException on a line with no visible cast proves that something somewhere produced an unchecked warning (or suppressed it). That is why you compile with -Xlint:unchecked and treat every suppression as a promise that you have proven.

code.title: Creating T instances and arrays

followUps: It uses the array's real class. Arrays.copyOf(T[] original, int n) calls original.getClass() and, if the class is not Object[], builds the new array with Array.newInstance(componentType, n). So copying a String[] gives a real String[] even though T is erased, because the runtime array object still knows its own element type. This works because arrays, unlike generics, are reified. The overload with a Class parameter does the same with a token you pass in.

A super type token is a trick to capture a full generic type like List<User> at runtime. You write an empty anonymous subclass new TypeReference<List<User>>() {}; its class file records TypeReference<List<User>> as the superclass, and reflection reads it. You need it when a plain Class is not enough, which happens whenever the type has type arguments: List.class says nothing about the elements. Jackson, Gson and Spring all offer one.

code.title: Super type token captures List<User>

followUps: The braces create an anonymous subclass, and only a subclass records its generic superclass in the class file. Without braces, new TypeReference<List<User>>() creates an instance of the base class itself, whose generic superclass is just Object, so the type argument was erased and cannot be recovered. Some libraries make the constructor protected or abstract so you cannot forget the braces.

Reflection reads generic signatures from declarations in several places. Dependency-injection frameworks such as Spring and Guice look at field.getGenericType() or constructor parameters to choose Repository<User> over Repository<Order>. ORMs read List<Order> fields to know the element entity, and REST frameworks read method return types to pick a JSON converter. All of it works because the Signature attribute survives erasure for fields, methods and class headers.

code.title: Type-safe heterogeneous container

followUps: Make the key bounded, for example Class<? extends Annotation>, and keep the generic method signature. <A extends Annotation> A get(Class<A> type) accepts Override.class but rejects String.class at compile time. This is how AnnotatedElement.getAnnotation works. The bound documents the family and prevents misuse, without losing the type-safe return value, which is still produced by type.cast(map.get(type)).

For thread safety, back it with a ConcurrentHashMap<Class<?>, Object> (it rejects null keys and values), or wrap access in a lock if you need check-then-act. The memory leak: the map holds strong references to Class objects, and a Class keeps its whole class loader alive. In an app server where web apps are redeployed, a long-lived container holding old classes prevents the loader from being collected. Fix with WeakHashMap keys or by removing entries on undeploy.

Reified generics would have broken the huge amount of existing code in 2004. Java 5 had to run with the same JVM and old libraries, and raw types like List were everywhere. If List<String> and List were distinct runtime classes, passing a raw list into new code would need conversions, and old jars could not use new generic classes. Erasure let one ArrayList.class serve both worlds. The trade-off was accepted knowingly.

A Kotlin inline fun <reified T> f() is inlined at each call site, so the compiler pastes the body there and replaces T with the real class known at that call. T::class and x is T then work, because the code contains the actual class, not a variable. It only works for inline functions; a normal generic function is still erased. The cost is code size, since the body is copied to every caller.
